issues.legal_issue: Claimants with proof of historical squatting must receive equal priority whether or not they possess the survey receipt.
material_facts: The existing scheme gave first priority to people found squatting during the specified historical period whose names appeared in a survey report, subject to scrutiny of their claims.

The municipal corporation separated claimants who possessed a survey receipt from those who lacked it but could provide satisfactory proof of historical squatting, and proposed considering the latter group afterward.
issues.conclusion: Both groups belong to the same priority category. Claimants without the receipt but with satisfactory proof must be considered alongside receipt-holders and arranged according to their respective seniority.
issues.legal_principle: The Court clarified the first-priority guideline in Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458: proof of the qualifying historical squatting, rather than possession of a particular receipt, determines inclusion in the priority category.

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify the implementation of a scheme for allocating permissions to street traders.
predicates.claimant_has_survey_receipt: A street trader seeking priority possesses the receipt issued in connection with the survey.
predicates.claimant_proves_historical_squatting: A street trader seeking priority provides satisfactory proof of squatting during the qualifying historical period.

issues.definition: When a court clarifies an allocation scheme and a claimant either holds the survey receipt or proves qualifying historical squatting, the claimant receives priority according to seniority without a separate class based on receipt possession.

issues.legal_issue: Existing express permission for a covered trading place cannot be withdrawn through the implementation procedure, while new covered permissions are unavailable to claimants who were not previously granted that facility; temporary weather covers are distinct from semi-permanent structures.
material_facts: The corporation stated that the scheme would provide open-to-sky trading spaces and would not grant covered spaces, kiosks, stalls, or shops.
Some traders had expressly been permitted covered trading facilities in the past.
The Court considered temporary tarpaulin covers or umbrellas necessary to protect traders from the weather, but distinguished them from semi-permanent covers.
issues.conclusion: The corporation may not change the nature of a trading permission that expressly included a covered facility. Claimants without such prior express permission are not entitled to a covered facility under the scheme. Temporary covers for protection from the weather are permissible, but a trader may be evicted for putting up a semi-permanent cover under that pretext; the temporary cover should be removed after business hours.
issues.legal_principle: In clarifying the scheme issued pursuant to Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458, the Court preserved previously granted express facilities while distinguishing temporary protection from a permanent or semi-permanent covered occupation.

rule.if: scheme_clarification_proceeding and (prior_express_covered_permission or no_prior_express_covered_permission) and (temporary_weather_cover_used or semi_permanent_cover_erected)

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify the implementation of a scheme governing permission to trade from fixed public spaces.
predicates.prior_express_covered_permission: A trader had previously been expressly permitted to use a covered trading place.
predicates.no_prior_express_covered_permission: A trader had not previously been expressly permitted to use a covered trading place.
predicates.temporary_weather_cover_used: A trader uses a temporary cover to protect against weather.
predicates.semi_permanent_cover_erected: A trader puts up a semi-permanent cover over the permitted trading area.

issues.definition: In a scheme-clarification proceeding, prior express permission for a covered place is preserved, new covered facilities are not granted to others, and only temporary weather protection is allowed rather than a semi-permanent structure.

issues.legal_issue: A trader who cannot reliably establish payment of past charges because receipts or records are unavailable may be given an alternative means of clearing those dues.
material_facts: The earlier guideline made permission for a later category of traders subject to availability of space and clearance of municipal dues.
The traders argued that many had not retained receipts and that the corporation could not readily verify its records over the relevant period.
The Court accepted that this difficulty could cause hardship.
issues.conclusion: Traders facing that difficulty may clear the dues through a lump-sum amount paid in quarterly instalments. If a trader defaults, the allotment may be cancelled after a reminder, and the next person in seniority may receive the space.
issues.legal_principle: The Court modified the implementation of the dues condition in the category-three guideline from Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458, to address the practical difficulty of proving past payments where receipts and verifiable records were unavailable.

rule.if: scheme_clarification_proceeding and category_three_trader and (payment_receipts_not_retained or municipal_records_difficult_to_verify)

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify the implementation of a scheme for granting trading permissions.
predicates.category_three_trader: The claimant is a trader in the scheme category whose permission is conditional on available space and clearance of municipal dues.
predicates.payment_receipts_not_retained: The trader has not retained receipts that would establish payment of past charges.
predicates.municipal_records_difficult_to_verify: The corporation faces practical difficulty verifying whether the trader paid the past charges.

issues.definition: A trader in the relevant scheme category who faces difficulty proving past payment because receipts are missing or records are hard to verify may clear the dues through quarterly instalments.

issues.legal_issue: A limited opportunity to submit a formal claim may be given to traders whose court cases were pending when the earlier scheme judgment was delivered and who had not applied to the verification committee.
material_facts: Some traders had petitions, appeals, or suits pending in court when the earlier judgment established the scheme.
Those traders had bona fide believed that their pending cases meant they did not need to file a formal claim with the committee.
The corporation did not object to extending the opportunity to that limited group.
issues.conclusion: Those claimants were allowed one month to file their claims with particulars and supporting material before the committee, which was to examine them; the committee could request a certified copy if in doubt.
issues.legal_principle: The Court granted a limited procedural accommodation while implementing the scheme clarified in Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458, based on the claimants’ bona fide misunderstanding and the corporation’s lack of objection.

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify and implement a scheme for scrutinizing street traders’ claims.
predicates.court_case_pending_at_scheme_cutoff: The trader had a petition, appeal, or suit pending when the earlier scheme judgment was delivered.
predicates.formal_scheme_claim_not_filed_due_to_bon: The trader had not filed a formal claim because the trader believed the pending court case made a separate application unnecessary.

issues.definition: A trader whose case was pending at the relevant scheme cutoff and who omitted a formal claim through a bona fide misunderstanding may submit that claim for committee scrutiny.

issues.legal_issue: Protection under the trading-permission scheme is confined to claimants who fall within one of its specified categories.
material_facts: The earlier judgment set out four categories of squatters and hawkers eligible for consideration under the scheme, including specified groups eligible for trading permission or licences.
The Court stated that claimants outside all four categories fell outside the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The directions apply to claimants within any of the four specified categories; those outside them have no right under the scheme and are not entitled to its protection.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the four-category framework laid down in Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458, including its provision that persons outside the first three categories could apply for hawking licences under section 420 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, for consideration on merit.

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify the implementation and reach of a scheme for street traders.
predicates.claimant_seeks_scheme_protection: A street trader claims the protections or benefits provided by the scheme.

issues.definition: In a proceeding clarifying the scheme, a trader seeking its protection is protected only if the trader falls within one of its specified categories.

issues.legal_issue: Pending litigation concerning claims covered by the scheme may be terminated once the scheme provides a process for scrutiny, while the corporation must preserve the status quo during verification and affected traders may seek directions if the corporation breaches the order.
material_facts: Claims under the scheme were awaiting scrutiny by the corporation’s committee.
Numerous petitions, appeals, special leave petitions, and suits concerning traders’ claims were pending in courts.
The Court considered those claimants protected by its order during verification and provided a means to seek directions if the corporation violated the order.
issues.conclusion: The pending proceedings were terminated and interim stays vacated. The corporation was to maintain the status quo until verification was complete; it could act to evict claimants whose claims were rejected only after the prescribed interval. No further litigation on behalf of traders would be entertained, but a trader governed by the order could apply for directions if the corporation violated it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the protection afforded by its implementation of the scheme in Saudan Singh v. NDMC, [1992] 2 SCC 458, and used its jurisdiction over the pending proceedings to terminate duplicative litigation while preserving compliance and verification safeguards.

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify and implement a scheme for scrutinizing street traders’ claims.
predicates.scheme_claims_await_verification: Claims by traders covered by the scheme remain to be examined by the designated committee.
predicates.related_court_cases_pending: Court proceedings concerning the traders’ claims remain pending.

issues.definition: When claims under a scheme remain to be verified and related court proceedings are pending, those proceedings may be terminated while the status quo is preserved during verification and an application remains available to address a breach of the court’s directions.

issues.legal_issue: The municipal corporation must prevent future encroachments from defeating protected traders’ rights and must also protect shopkeepers’ interests.
material_facts: The Court’s order protected existing traders governed by the scheme while their claims were scrutinized.
The Court noted that future encroachments could defeat the rights of those traders.
The Court also noted that shopkeepers had a similar right under Article 21 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The corporation was directed to prevent future encroachments that would defeat the rights of traders governed by the scheme and to protect the interests of shopkeepers.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Article 21 of the Constitution in recognizing the interests of shopkeepers and directed the corporation to balance those interests with the rights of traders protected under the scheme.

predicates.scheme_clarification_proceeding: The court was asked to clarify the implementation of a scheme governing street traders.
predicates.existing_traders_protected: Traders governed by the scheme are protected while their claims are considered.
predicates.future_encroachment_may_defeat_protected: A future encroachment could defeat the rights of traders protected under the scheme.

issues.definition: When a scheme-clarification proceeding protects existing traders and future encroachments could defeat their rights, the corporation must prevent those encroachments while protecting shopkeepers’ interests.
